Le 4 novembre dernier, j’étais à l’Ausga: Last November 4, I was at the Ausgang Plaza on Saint-Hubert Street. The room was packed to the rafters: activists, artists, researchers and ordinary citizens – women and men who had come to attend a debate titled “Does Immigration Threaten Secularism?” The organizers were offering a chance to better understand these two concepts and the relationship between them through the lens of current events in Quebec.
Entre les prises de parole et les presta: Between the speeches and the applauded artistic performances, I met a community determined to defend a vision of Quebec that brings together freedom, equality and difference.
J’ai discuté avec des femmes qui portent: I spoke with women who wear the veil, with activists, with legal experts. Their words speak of fear, vigilance, solidarity.
<strong>L’immigration menace-t-elle la l: Does immigration threaten secularism in Quebec? That was the question posed on November 4 at the Ausgang Plaza, where more than 150 people gathered to reflect, debate and resist. With talks, poetry, comedy and militant rap, the evening, organized as part of the Mois d’action pour la justice migrante, was meant as an act of resistance against the “identity-politics one-upmanship taking hold in Quebec as the provincial election approaches.”

Les discours, les lois, les chiffres rés: The speeches, the laws, the numbers resonate with real lives. Those of <l1>Muslim women resisting the fallout of Bill 21</l1>, like Mounia Malouf.
Mounia a fait le déplacement depuis la v: Mounia travelled from Québec City to attend this event organized by the Ligue des droits et libertés (LDL) and the Observatoire pour la justice migrante (OPLJM). A teacher in her country of origin, she says she had to change careers to head off the effects of Bill 21 and, now, Bill 94, which restricts women who wear the hijab from accessing certain professions in Quebec. “I knew it was coming with the previous laws and the one that was just passed [Bill 94, ed.]. So I wanted to take a different professional path to avoid the social shock,” she explains. After completing training in early childhood education, Mounia ultimately chose to work for an organization rather than pursue her calling as a teacher.
Au fond de la salle, adossée au mur, ell: At the back of the room, leaning against the wall, she listens closely, mulls over the criticisms raised by the panellists and talks with other committed women who are defending their rights as Quebec women. “My normal life is my hijab,” she says. “I will never give up that part of myself just because it’s a religious symbol.”
Dans sa vie quotidienne, le constat est: In her daily life, the reality is even harsher for Mounia. Insults, slurs and experiences of systemic racism punctuate her movements around the city, she confides – and she is not the only one who endures this. She points out that the people around her, mostly Muslim women who wear the hijab, face a rising tide of hatred expressed as much in looks as in actions.
La salle, où plus de 150 personnes se pr: The room, where more than 150 people are crowded together, is packed. The chairs are squeezed tight, and the air is a little heavy after four hours of discussion. Throughout the evening, expert panels and artistic performances follow one another. In the audience, people recognize each other, listen to each other, laugh at times, applaud often.
Il y a des étudiants, des militantes, de: There are students, activists, researchers, but also well-known figures from the progressive scene, such as MNA Haroun Bouazzi and rapper Webster. The atmosphere is both studious and fraternal, driven by a shared feeling: the desire to resist fear.
Avant de passer la parole aux panélistes: Before handing the floor to the panellists, LDL coordinator Laurence Guénette sets the scene: that of a Quebec shaped by “rampant Islamophobia” and a series of laws adopted “in the name of a secularism that is harmful to rights and freedoms.” She recalls that the LDL and the OPLJM have mobilized together against Bills C-2 and C-12 in Ottawa, but also against Bill 94, recently passed in Québec City, which notably bans the wearing of religious symbols for certain women working in the education network.
« Il faut le dire clairement : ce sont d: “We have to say it clearly: lives are at stake. Discrimination is not just abstract debate,” says Ms.<sup> </sup>Guénette. A silence falls over the room when she mentions the recent death of Shandi Cook, a young Indigenous woman who died in Manitoba after being refused care.
La lumière se tamise. Sur l’écran, une<l: The lights dim. On the screen, a<l1> video</l1> poses the question that will be the thread running through the evening: “Does immigration really threaten secularism?”
En quelques minutes, les voix de l’autri: In a few minutes, the voices of author Kev Lambert, law professor Louis-Philippe Lampron and activist Amel Zaazaa dissect, with biting humour, the political logic behind the proliferation of bills on secularism and the obsessive reactions around the hijab. “If we had to fill a pothole every time someone talks about the Islamic veil, Quebec would have some damn fine roads!” we hear. In the room, a few discreet laughs break out.
Une autre voix conclut : « À force de ch: Another voice concludes: “By dint of looking for a scapegoat, isn’t the state crucifying its own secularism?”
Sur scène, le juriste Pierre Bosset rapp: On stage, legal scholar Pierre Bosset reminds the audience from the outset that secularism, in its original sense, concerns the state and its institutions, not individuals. In his view, Quebec confuses secularization with secularism, and this confusion legitimizes political excesses. Bill 21 is not a law on secularism, Mr. Bosset argues; “it’s a law that bans the wearing of religious symbols for certain categories of state agents, [...] especially women teachers.”
L’intervenant critiquera aussi la loi 94: He also criticizes Bill 94, which extends to students the requirement to have their faces uncovered at school. This, he says, is a “worrying distortion of the very notion of secularism, since it’s as if students were supposed to be secular, when in reality, what must be secular is the state.” Finally, he concludes, the debate is really about the use of the notwithstanding clause. This mechanism, he explains, creates “a dangerous precedent, because it allows the violation of equality between men and women under the cover of neutrality.”
L’historien et membre de la LDL Paul-Éti: Historian and LDL member Paul-Étienne Rainville places the debate in a longer arc: that of a Quebec “where Catholic culture long served as a pillar of the colonial project.”
Selon lui, « la laïcité qu’on présente c: In his view, “the secularism presented as a Quebec value is a historical aberration.” He notes that freedom-curtailing laws targeting certain religious minorities “already existed in the Duplessis years,” and that the identity-driven turn begun in the 2000s “is a continuation of survivance nationalism.”
Pour M. Rainville, la loi 21 et les disc: For Mr. Rainville, Bill 21 and the talk of “Quebec values” reflect a shift: “We went from this idea of secularism that would guarantee individuals’ fundamental freedoms to this idea of laicism, which in fact sought to limit the exercise of the fundamental freedoms of certain groups, and in particular of Muslims.”
Pour la juriste Dania Suliman, les débat: For legal scholar Dania Suliman, debates on secularism and “reasonable accommodation” in Quebec are often skewed. She points out that in practice, it is mostly people from the Christian majority who benefit from time off or exemptions tied to their religion (Christmas or Easter, for example, are already part of the official calendar). Minorities, for their part, have to request “accommodations” to celebrate their holidays, which puts them in a position of exception from the outset. An exception that Bill 94 has just shut the door on, she says, by banning, among other things, halal meat in schools and days off for religious holidays such as Eid or Chinese New Year. She suggests instead talking about “real equality”: offering everyone the same recognition, whatever their beliefs.
De son côté, la professeure Leïla Benhad: For her part, Professor Leïla Benhadjoudja places the secularism debate in a broader context. In her view, the way Quebec draws on the French model perpetuates a colonial view of the world: one that associates the majority religion with progress, and other traditions with difference or suspicion. For her, secularism thus becomes a political tool used to control racialized minorities, especially Muslim women.
Dans une intervention vibrante, la cherc: In a stirring address, researcher and professor Zeinab Diab, who was forced to leave Quebec because of Bill 21, described the law as “an instrument of racial and sexist control, hidden under the veneer of secularism.” Drawing on <l1>her thesis</l1> as well as on 21 interviews she conducted with Muslim women in Quebec as part of her research, she highlights the “social deaths” this law produces: job loss, fear, invisibilization and more. But behind the pain, Ms. Diab sees resistance emerging: these women are turning their hijab and their voices into political acts of survival and dignity. “Listen to us, we don’t need to be saved. We know what we want,” she says.

Pour M<sup>me </sup>Diab, la laïcité « n: For Ms.<sup> </sup>Diab, secularism “is not neutral” when it leads to the exclusion of veiled women from the labour market. She points to “the symbolic violence” of a society that claims to protect women while shutting them out of public spaces.
La directrice de l’Observatoire, Amel Za: The Observatoire’s director, Amel Zaazaa, stresses how much the question of secularism is being exploited to construct “the figure of the immigrant as a threat.”
Elle rappelle que les travailleurs migra: She points out that temporary foreign workers, international students and asylum seekers contribute to the economy and to the funding of the social system, while being largely excluded from it. “Immigration takes the blame for everything,” she observes. “It’s practically the government’s Swiss Army knife: every time something fails, they brandish immigration.”
Pour elle, la rhétorique gouvernementale: For her, the government’s rhetoric turns immigration into a scapegoat. “During the pandemic, we celebrated essential workers. Today, we accuse them of harming access to health care or housing. It’s deeply hypocritical,” she says.
Malgré les attaques, la société civile n: Despite the attacks, civil society isn’t done yet. “We’re forming a broad front: unions, community organizations, NGOs, artists…” lists Amel Zaazaa. Despite “the freeze on community funding and the bills that weaken unions” – aimed at “reducing our power to act” – a surge of unity seems to be emerging, says the Observatoire’s director. “Ten years ago, demands like status for all were divisive. Today, we find ourselves in the same struggles. We no longer have a choice,” she says. For her, evenings like this one are essential: “It’s in these spaces that we rebuild counterpower. Where words circulate, where alliances are made.”
Abordant le même thème, des performances: Addressing the same theme, artistic performances extend the evening. On stage, poet Marilou Craft delivers a text on dignity and memory. Comedians Emna Achour and Coralie LaPerrière shake up clichés through laughter. Then rapper Webster closes the evening with a new track: Résistance, dedicated to Palestine. The crowd chants the chorus in unison.
Quand, vers la fin, une animatrice inter: Near the end, when a host interrupts the program to announce the election of Zohran Mamdani, the young socialist and son of immigrants, as mayor of New York, a roar shakes the room. Like a nod to the world people would like to see here too: fairer, more open, more hopeful.
Les participants se dispersent lentement: Participants disperse slowly. Contact details are exchanged, along with promises of joint action. Mounia heads home from Montréal with a quiet smile. “Yes, there is hate,” she acknowledges. “But there is also solidarity. And we don’t say that enough.”
